data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A test constrains its subject rather than describes it only when the test's failure condition is causally upstream of the subject's implementation choices, so that the author shapes the subject to make the test pass. When the test is written after the subject and merely records its behaviour, the test describes. The 3-of-26 result is a consequence of the same author writing both the subject and the test in the same week: the author's own guard-writing ritual constrains only the mutations the author anticipated, while 23 of 26 mutations fall outside the author's anticipated failure space and are merely described.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The author's guards were written to a specification independent of any particular failure, so anticipation capture does not apply","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The 3-of-26 result is explained by the small mutation sample size and would not replicate in a larger mutation set","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"A test constrains its subject whenever it is a necessary condition for merge, independent of author anticipation or temporal ordering","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism is 'anticipation capture': an author who writes a guard after observing a specific failure will only constrain mutations that reproduce that specific failure mode. The shown-to-fail-first ritual narrows the author's attention to the planted failure, so the guard's predicate is shaped by the author's expectation of what can fail, not by the subject's actual failure surface. The distribution is explained by the number of mutation types that match the author's anticipated failure template versus those that do not.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
